title: Inflection-point Prober: lightweight runtime that detects kernel performance crossovers for arch/seq-length adaptation
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Goal: build and validate a low-overhead "inflection-point prober" subsystem that 1) inserts micro-probes into live traffic to detect sequence-length and architecture-driven performance crossovers between candidate kernels, 2) maintains a compact per-model 'performance sketch' that captures inflection points (seqlen and batch-size thresholds) and 3) feeds an online heuristic that flips kernel choices only when statistically significant wins are observed and safety constraints (latency SLOs, cold-start risk) are met.

Motivation and context:
- Existing heuristics use coarse buckets or offline profiling; they miss runtime shifts caused by mixed tenant traffic, model updates, or GPU-specific microarchitecture differences.
- We want continuous adaptation with bounded probe overhead and no visible spike in p99 latency.

Design summary:
- Probe mechanism: occasionally tag a small fraction of eligible requests (0.5% - 2%) as probes and route them to alternate kernel candidates in parallel or serially depending on risk budget. Probes are rate-limited by per-POD and per-model budgets.
- Inflection detection: maintain a decaying histogram of per-token throughput and tail latency mapped by (seqlen_bucket, batch_size, gpu_arch). Periodically compute a crossover score for each pair of kernels using bootstrap CI to determine significance.
- Performance sketch: compact string-key map keyed by model:kernel_pair:arch:seqlen_bucket that stores median throughput ratio, p99 delta, sample counts, last_probe_ts. Sketch stored in-memory with periodic checkpointing to Redis for cluster-wide warmstart.
- Safety and rollback: require a minimum sample count (default 50 probes) and positive throughput win >= 1.07x and p99 not worse than +5ms before committing a persistent kernel switch. If a recent switch increases error rates or spikes p99, trigger automatic rollback and mark kernel pair as 'unstable' for a cool-down window.
- Scheduler integration: prober hooks into prefill/decode scheduler. For prefill-heavy requests we prefer parallel probing (shadow execution) when resources permit; for tail-sensitive decode we use serial probing with small sample sizes.

Acceptance criteria:
- Net probe CPU/GPU overhead across mixed benchmark <= 0.8% ideally <0.5% for production mixes.
- No increase in 95th/99th latency >5% in baseline workloads during steady state.
- Performance sketch can predict the correct kernel >90% of time for held-out sequences in A/B tests.

Measured results (early experiments):
- Small experiment run 2025-02-24 on a 4-node cluster (A100-80GB and H100) using convai and longform workloads:
  * A100, model rdl-7B (int8), seqlen 16-64: current kernel K1 median throughput=520 tok/s, kernel K2=560 tok/s (+7.7%), p99 +1.2ms. Probe overhead 0.3% CPU.
  * H100, same model, seqlen 256: K1=260 tok/s, K2=195 tok/s (-25%), prober detected crossover and avoided costly switch due to negative sign.
  * Mixed production trace (10k requests): prober tagging at 1% led to 0.45% additional GPU-util and no observable p99 regression.

Trade-offs discussed:
- Probe frequency vs. signal latency: higher probe rates surface changes faster but increase overhead and tail risk. We plan adaptive probe rate: initial ramp (1-2%) then decay to 0.2% once confidence>95%.
- Shadow (parallel) vs serial probing: parallel gives cleaner signal but doubles inference cost for probed requests; restrict to low-cost prefill requests or opportunistic idle capacity.
- State sharing: Redis checkpointing enables warm starts across pods but has staleness risk; include last_probe_ts and soft TTL to prevent relying on stale sketches.

Open implementation tasks (this ticket):
- Implement probe tagging API in request router and add prober metadata to request trace.
- Build compact PerformanceSketch store with Redis checkpoint/restore and eviction policy.
- Add bootstrap CI test harness for small-sample significance testing (with synthetic workload generator).
- Integrate safety checks into scheduler: p99 guardrails and automatic rollback triggers.
- Instrumentation dashboards (Console) that show per-model inflection curves and probe health metrics.

Non-goals:
- Full offline autotuner or global bandit optimizer. We aim for a lightweight runtime probe + heuristic switcher.

Rollout plan:
1) Canary cluster only accept internal traffic, probe rate 2%, shadow-only for prefill. Measure for 2 weeks.
2) Gradually enable serial probes for decode in low-risk models and reduce probe rate.
3) Controlled ramp to production with per-customer opt-out flag and telemetry.

Risks and mitigation:
- Multi-tenant fairness: excessive probes could unfairly allocate GPU time. Mitigation: global per-GPU probe throttle and tenant-aware budgets.
- False positives due to transient queueing: mitigate using decaying histograms and min-samples before commit.
- Interaction with quantized fallbacks: ensure probes compare matching quantization paths or explicitly tag quantization variant.

Related artifacts and links:
- Design doc: https://docs.internal.redwood.ai/confluence/runtime/inflection-prober (proto)
- Perf harness repo PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime-perf/pull/189
- Experimental dashboard: https://grafana.internal.redwood.ai/d/inflection-prober/overview

Next steps for this ticket:
- Diego: land probe tagging and basic sketch store (ETA 1 week).
- Ava: implement bootstrap CI test harness + synthetic generator (ETA 10 days).
- Infra: provision Redis namespace for sketch checkpointing and set up retention policy.

Notes: this ticket intentionally focuses on the runtime probe and heuristic switcher. If experiments show strong stability and low overhead we'll follow up with a separate ticket to build a continuous bandit-style autotuner that optimizes probe budgets and multi-kernel portfolios.
